t.1.147.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having heard that excessive speech of the two grief-stricken ones, the daughter, her limbs utterly overwhelmed with sorrow, addressed them both.
t.1.147.2: Why do you two, sorely afflicted with grief, wail like those who have no protector? Hear something from me as well, and having heard it, let what is fitting be done.
t.1.147.3: By dharma I am the one you two must give up; of this there is no doubt. By giving me up, since I am the one to be abandoned, everything is saved by me alone.
t.1.147.5: A son should rescue his father from hardship, whether here in this world or after he has departed; in every way a son should rescue him, and that is why the wise call him a son.
t.1.147.4: Offspring is desired for this very purpose, with the thought, 'It will carry me across.' Now that the time has come, cross over by means of me, as if by a boat.
t.1.147.7: And this little brother of mine, once you have gone to that other world, would perish in a very short time; there is no doubt.
t.1.147.6: The forefathers, too, always long for daughters' sons; I myself shall surely save them by protecting my father's life.
t.1.147.8: For when father has gone to heaven and my younger brother has perished, the funeral offering of rice to the ancestors would be cut off, and that would be displeasing to them.
t.1.147.9: Abandoned by my father, and likewise by my mother and my brother, I would without doubt die, having passed from sorrow into greater sorrow, I who am not accustomed to such a lot.
t.1.147.10: But if you are set free unharmed, then my mother and my infant brother, our lineage and the ancestral offering too, will without doubt stand secure.
t.1.147.11: A son is one's own self, a wife is a friend, but a daughter, they say, is a burden. So free yourself from this burden, and unite me with dharma.
t.1.147.12: Bereft of you, father, I shall become an unprotected, wretched young girl, drifting wherever chance may take me. Alas, how pitiable I shall be!
t.1.147.13: Or rather, I shall bring about the deliverance of this family; having done a deed most difficult to do, I shall attain the fruit of it.
t.1.147.14: Or if you go there, abandoning me, O best of the twice-born, I shall be afflicted; consider that, and consider me too.
t.1.147.15: Therefore, O best of good men, for our sake, for the sake of dharma, and for the sake of offspring, protect yourself, and give me up, for I am the one who ought to be given up.
t.1.147.16: In a matter that must surely be done, let not this time pass you by; and through the water offered by you, good will come to me as well.
t.1.147.17: What greater sorrow could there be than this, that once you have gone to heaven, we should run about like dogs, begging food from others?
t.1.147.19: Having heard her lament of many kinds in this way, the father, the mother, and that maiden too, all three, burst into tears.
t.1.147.18: But when you, safe and well together with your kinsmen, are freed from this affliction, I, dwelling in the world of the immortals, shall be filled with happiness.
t.1.147.20: Then, hearing them all weeping, the son of those two, a little boy with wide-open eyes, spoke sweetly and indistinctly.
t.1.147.22: Then, picking up a blade of grass, he joyfully spoke again: "With this I shall kill that man-eating Rākṣasa."
t.1.147.23: Even so, though they were overwhelmed by grief, when they heard that indistinct speech of the little boy, a great joy arose among them.
t.1.147.21: Saying, “Do not weep, father; do not, mother; do not you, sister,” he moves from one to another among them all, as if smiling.
t.1.147.24: Knowing that this was the right moment, Kuntī approached them and, as though reviving with nectar those whose life had departed, spoke these words.
